newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat profits slump as margins tumble.
newsitem.headline: Fiat profits slump as margins tumble.

text.p: Italian automotive giant Fiat Monday reported a 36 percent slide in profits for the first nine months of 1996 as profit margins were squeezed hard by lingering market difficulties.

Italy's biggest private industrial group reported pretax profits in the nine months to end-September fell to 1.759 trillion lire ($1.2 billion) from 2.743 trillion lire ($1.8 billion). Its overall revenues rose 4 percent to 57.918 trillion lire ($38.3 billion).
Fiat blamed the fall in profitability on the depressed Italian car market, lower demand for industrial trucks and the strong lira's effect on exports from the Turin-based group.

Group nine-month operating profits slid to 1.706 trillion lire ($1.12 billion), equal to a profit margin of 2.9 percent, compared to 2.513 trillion lire ($1.7 billion), or 4.5 percent margin, in the year-ago period.
"Clearly, profit margins are under great pressure. There is usually a seasonal drop in margins in the third quarter but this is a lot worse than expected," said one industry analyst.
He calculated that Fiat's profit margin had sunk to 1.1 percent in the third quarter (July-September) from 3.8 percent during the first half of 1996.
Fiat said it had responsed to difficult market conditions by containing production, reducing inventory, increasing efficiency and cutting costs.
These factors had a negative impact on current results but should have a positive effect for the future, Fiat said.
The group's car division, Fiat Auto, recorded sales up 5.2 percent at 1.74 million cars in the nine month period, with sales to European nations outside Italy rising by 108,000.
Fiat's truck division, Iveco, said vehicle sales were up 1 percent to 86,700 trucks with its share of the European market rising 2 percentage points to 20.2 percent.

Its New Holland unit, the world's number one tractor maker and number two in the farm machinery group after U.S. John Deere, saw tractors sales fall 3.7 percent to 61,400 as the group tried to offer a full range of new models while it suffered from a poor Brazilian market.

The group said that the nine-month results came before the sale of its fund management arm Prime to insurer Generali and the flotation of around 30 percent of New Holland on the New York stock market. Last year, results were boosted by the sale of Fiat's CEAC battery business for 380 billion lire ($215.1 million).
